notes.meaning: Jabin king of Hazor heard how Israel conquered southern Canaan and sent messengers to call other northern kings together. Hazor was the largest and most powerful inland city in the north, so its king took the lead in organizing resistance. Facing a growing threat, he wanted a united front to stop Israel.

Jabin summoned rulers from the northern mountains, the plains south of the Sea of Galilee, the coastal lowlands, and Dor in the west. He also called together several Canaanite peoples living between the Mediterranean Sea and the foothills of Mount Hermon. This brought almost all of northern Canaan into a single large alliance against Israel.

The allied kings marched out with an enormous army described as being as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They also brought many horses and war chariots, which were the heaviest and most terrifying weapons of that era. Israel had not faced chariots before, making this their greatest military test so far.

All the northern kings gathered and set up camp by the waters of Merom to attack Israel together. Merom was a water basin in Upper Galilee located not far from Hazor. Gathering there allowed the allied forces to unite their troops and chariots before marching into battle.

The Lord told Joshua not to fear their huge numbers or advanced equipment, promising total victory by the next day. God commanded Israel to hamstring the enemy horses by cutting their leg tendons and to burn the chariots with fire. This prevented Israel from building a chariot army so they would always rely on God rather than weapons.

Joshua led his army quickly and launched a surprise attack against the coalition at the waters of Merom. Striking suddenly caught the allied kings off guard before they could deploy their chariots on flat ground. God blessed their bold action and gave them the upper hand right away.

The Lord handed the enemy armies over to Israel, who routed them and chased the fleeing troops far to the west and east. The pursuit went as far as the coastal city of Sidon and eastward to the valley of Mizpeh. Israel wiped out the enemy army so completely that no survivors remained to fight back.

Joshua carried out every detail of what the Lord had ordered concerning the enemy equipment. He disabled the horses and burned up the chariots rather than keeping them for Israel's military power. True obedience means following God's commands even when worldly advantages are left behind.

After the pursuit, Joshua turned back and captured the city of Hazor, putting its king to death. Hazor was singled out because it was the chief capital that had organized and led the northern rebellion. Bringing down its king broke the main center of power in northern Canaan.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists have confirmed Hazor was a major fortified city destroyed by fire in the 13th century B.C., though scholars debate whether the destruction was caused by Israelites, Sea Peoples, or rival Canaanites.

notes.meaning: The Israelites executed all the people inside Hazor under God's judgment and burned the city to the ground. Hazor was one of only three cities in Canaan that Joshua destroyed by fire, along with Jericho and Ai. Burning it served as a clear sign that its reign over the region was finished.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that while Hazor was burned during this era, the destruction could have been carried out by Egypt, the Sea Peoples, or a rival Canaanite power, though Joshua remains a possible cause.

notes.meaning: Joshua went on to take all the other cities that belonged to the allied kings, capturing their rulers and putting the inhabitants to death. He devoted them to destruction just as Moses had commanded from the Lord. Joshua was acting as an agent carrying out God's legal judgment rather than pursuing personal revenge.

Israel left the other cities standing on their ancient mounds and did not burn them, destroying only Hazor by fire. Towns built on raised mounds were easily defended and useful for Israel to live in later. Hazor alone was burned because it had ignited the war against God's people.

The Israelites kept the goods and farm animals from these captured towns as plunder for themselves. However, they struck down all the human inhabitants until the population was completely wiped out. This followed the instructions God had given Moses regarding the corrupt Canaanite nations.

The Lord had given commands to Moses, Moses had passed them on to Joshua, and Joshua obeyed them without leaving anything undone. The report highlights Joshua's complete faithfulness to the written law of God. Faithful leaders pass on God's truth and carry it out with whole hearts.

Joshua took control of the entire territory, including the southern desert, the central highlands, the western foothills, and the northern mountains. The conquered land stretched from Mount Halak near Edom in the far south all the way to Baal-gad at Mount Hermon in the north. Israel broke the organized power of every Canaanite king across the whole land.

The campaign against all these kings took a long time to finish, lasting about five to seven years. Although the open-field battles were swift, laying siege to well-defended walled cities required years of steady effort. God fulfills His promises according to His own wise schedule.

Not a single city reached a peaceful agreement with Israel except the Hivite inhabitants of Gibeon. Every other town chose to resist and had to be taken in battle. The Canaanite rulers stubbornly fought against Israel rather than seeking mercy or acknowledging Israel's God.

The Lord hardened the hearts of the Canaanites so they would march out to battle and face destruction without mercy. God did this by giving them over to their own persistent pride and rebellion, bringing about the judgment He had commanded Moses to execute. God's justice firmly punishes deep-rooted wickedness after giving long periods of warning.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teachers such as Origen interpreted the hardening and destruction of Canaanite enemies spiritually, seeing it as a symbol for wiping out every sinful desire in the Christian soul.

notes.meaning: Joshua also drove out the Anakim, a tall and fearsome people who had terrified the Israelite spies forty years earlier. He destroyed their strongholds in Hebron, Debir, and across the hill country, leaving none alive in Israel's land. A small remnant survived only along the coast in the Philistine cities of Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod.

Joshua secured control over the whole land just as the Lord had promised to Moses. He prepared to give the land to the tribes of Israel as their permanent inheritance, and the land finally enjoyed rest from war. God proved faithful to His promise, giving His people security and peace.
